summary.text: At \(n=140\), exact rational bounds on \(\sqrt{5/4}\) give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus the claimed relation would require \(542=528+484-471=541\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor,
 \qquad n\ge 1.
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
 a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by taking \(n=140\). Thus the four terms that must be evaluated are
\(a(140),a(144),a(157)\), and \(a(161)\).

We first determine all four square-root floor terms exactly. Put
\[
 \alpha=\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
For positive integers \(m\) and nonnegative integers \(q\), the inequalities
\[
 4q^2\le 5m^2<4(q+1)^2
\]
imply
\[
 q\le m\alpha<q+1.
\]
Indeed, after division by the positive number \(4m^2\), the displayed squared inequalities become
\[
 \left(\frac qm\right)^2\le \frac54<
 \left(\frac{q+1}{m}\right)^2.
\]
All quantities involved are nonnegative, so taking square roots preserves their order. Multiplication by \(m>0\) then gives
\(q\le m\alpha<q+1\), and hence
\[
 \lfloor m\alpha\rfloor=q.
\]
We apply this observation separately to each of the four required indices.

For \(m=140\) and \(q=156\), direct integer arithmetic gives
\[
 5\cdot 140^2-4\cdot156^2=656>0
\]
and
\[
 4\cdot157^2-5\cdot140^2=596>0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 4\cdot156^2<5\cdot140^2<4\cdot157^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
 156<140\alpha<157,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor140\alpha\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Consequently,
\[
 a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

For \(m=144\) and \(q=160\), we have
\[
 5\cdot144^2-4\cdot160^2=1280>0
\]
and
\[
 4\cdot161^2-5\cdot144^2=4>0.
\]
Thus
\[
 4\cdot160^2<5\cdot144^2<4\cdot161^2,
\]
so
\[
 160<144\alpha<161,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor144\alpha\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(144/4=36\), it follows that
\[
 a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(m=157\) and \(q=175\), the corresponding integer differences are
\[
 5\cdot157^2-4\cdot175^2=745>0
\]
and
\[
 4\cdot176^2-5\cdot157^2=659>0.
\]
Hence
\[
 4\cdot175^2<5\cdot157^2<4\cdot176^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
 175<157\alpha<176,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor157\alpha\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Furthermore, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), so
\(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). We obtain
\[
 a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(m=161\) and \(q=180\), we find
\[
 5\cdot161^2-4\cdot180^2=5>0
\]
and
\[
 4\cdot181^2-5\cdot161^2=1439>0.
\]
It follows that
\[
 4\cdot180^2<5\cdot161^2<4\cdot181^2,
\]
whence
\[
 180<161\alpha<181,
 \qquad
 \left\lfloor161\alpha\right\rfloor=180.
\]
Because \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we also have
\(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Thus
\[
 a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

Now substitute \(n=140\) into the conjectured recurrence. Its left-hand side is
\[
 a(140+21)=a(161)=542.
\]
Its right-hand side is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 a(140+17)+a(140+4)-a(140)
 &=a(157)+a(144)-a(140)\\
 &=528+484-471\\
 &=541.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus this instance of the proposed identity asserts \(542=541\), which is false. Since \(140\ge1\), this is an admissible index in the universally quantified conjecture. Therefore the conjecture that
\(a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)\) for every \(n\ge1\) is disproved.
